newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - NZ's Countrywide grows by tapping niches.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - NZ's Countrywide grows by tapping niches.

text.p: New Zealand's Countrywide Banking Corporation is set to report a strong rise in first-half profit and will build on its successful strategy of exploiting niche opportunities, Managing Director David Wolfenden said on Friday.
The group, owned by Bank of Scotland, has just launched its latest such venture -- an asset financing company to finance plant equipment and heavy vehicles for medium-size businesses.
Wolfenden expects the month-old company, Capital Equipment Finance Ltd, to generate business worth around NZ$60 million in the next 12 months and at least $300 million a year within five years.
The nature of the business was such that contributions were often better than from core activities where margins were very tight.
"It's one way of diversifying our risk and improving our revenues," he said in an interview.
"We're not in the rural sector, we're not in corporate banking, so we are actually specific, and our whole thrust is to be market leader in segments that we're actually in."
Countrywide is due to report for the six months to August 31 in a couple of weeks.

"It will show very strong growth for us again, which is consistent with the growth we've shown in the last couple of years," Wolfenden said, adding growth was driven by higher volume in the face of contracting margins.
"Our actual growth performance and our profit performance is significantly up on the comparable half-year."
Countrywide reported tax-paid profit of NZ$42 million in the year to February 29. Its net after tax profit for the six months to August 31, 1995 was NZ$21 million.

Wolfenden said Countrywide was "reasonably comfortable" with its network of 70 branches in New Zealand but was keeping that number under review given trends towards smart cards, telephone banking and use of the Internet.

He said "only a fool" would ignore the entrance to the market of non-bank institutions whose lack of branch overheads enabled them to offer competitive mortgage rates, an example being fund manager AMP's Ergo subsidiary.
"I think the banking industry will have to meet that head on," Wolfenden said. "The traditional role of banks is changing, and changing rapidly."
He said it was no secret that Bank of Scotland had been interested in Trust Bank New Zealand, which was bought by Westpac Banking Corp earlier this year.
But Bank of Scotland remained strongly committed to Australasia, with 21 percent of its capital invested here through its ownership of Countrywide and 51 percent of Perth-based Bank West.
Countrywide has recently set up a small Hong Kong operation to handle all its offshore funding and develop links with Asia.
Wolfenden said some Asian businessmen were hesitating about long-term investment in New Zealand because of the uncertain political climate in the run-up to the October 12 election.
The left-wing Alliance and economic nationalist New Zealand First are both hostile to asset sales to foreign interests.

"Asian entrepreneurs like certainty. They like stability and they like certainty...New Zealand is giving them a perception of being unsure about providing the stability and certainty that they require to make long-term investment decisions."

He said Countrywide's ongoing fund raising programme in Asia would continue on a needs basis. The bank earlier this year raised US$249 million through an Asian floating rate note issue that was fully subscribed by Hong Kong and Singapore investors.
Wolfenden said financial markets can expect a period of uncertainty after the election, and he saw little scope for the Reserve Bank to ease monetary policy before the first quarter of next year.
